paragraphs.text: BOOK ONE

Good speech, full of prudence, is necessary to everyone for instruction, and a mind intent on reason leads the way to the virtues and restrains the passions; for virtue can be taught. Indeed, it is sought through study and learning, and lost through neglect. Otherwise, if good speech were not necessary for correction, the law would never say: You shall not commit adultery. But because bare speech is useful for warning but weak for persuading, the consideration of right reason must be brought in, so that what good speech has prescribed, reason, more fully worked out, may persuade. For we are not bound to obey by a slave's necessity, but by the free choice of the will, whether we lean toward virtue or incline toward fault. And so either our unfettered feelings draw us into error, or the will, following reason, calls us back. Now the most grievous passion leading to fault is concupiscence, which reason softens and represses. It can soften it, but it cannot uproot it, since the mind, which is capable of reason, is not the master of its passions but their restrainer. For it is not possible for someone quick to anger not to become angry; what is possible is that he temper himself by reason, hold back his indignation and keep himself from punishing, as the prophet also teaches us, saying: Be angry, and do not sin. He granted what belongs to nature and forbade what belongs to fault.

Every [?], therefore, takes its origin from other things, not from itself, and so it is secondary. For it is concerned either with natural things or with useful things; thus it either moderates what is natural or champions what is useful. In short, it does not cut desire out of the soul, but ensures that we do not become slaves to desire. For who is great enough to take away the impulses of the body, except him alone who could say of the barren fig tree, that is, of the wickedness of the Jews: Look, for three years now I have come looking for fruit on this fig tree and find none; so cut it down. His servant answered him: Leave it this year too, until I dig around it and put on a basket of manure. And if it bears fruit, well and good; but if not, cut it down in the future. He rightly referred the matter to his master, because he could not claim for himself the power to cut away the body's falling into sin, but left it to the Lord.

Indeed, whom among men shall we take as better and braver than holy David? He could not rid himself of the craving with which he longed for water from the cistern of Bethlehem, cut off by the enemy army, but he could moderate it. We do not find that water was lacking to the others, that is, to so large an army, and surely it could much less have been lacking to the king, since there were other springs; yet, suffering a kind of irrational craving, he longed for that water which was hemmed in by the enemy encircling it, and from which it could not easily have been brought without the greatest danger. So he said: Who will give me a drink from the cistern that is in Bethlehem by the gate? And when three men were found to cut through the enemy camp and bring back the water he had longed for so intensely, he recognized that this water had cost others their peril, and he poured it out to the Lord, so as not to seem to drink the blood of those who had brought it. This shows that desire does outrun reason, but that reason resists craving. David, then, suffered something human in desiring irrationally; but what is praiseworthy is that he cheated his irrational desire with a remedy rationally prepared. While I praise the men who were ashamed at their king's desire and preferred to put an end to his embarrassment even at the risk of their own lives, I praise more the one who, in his own desire, was ashamed of another's danger, and counted the water, obtained at the price of an uncertain fate, as equal to blood. At the same time, as victor over the craving he had subdued, he poured the water out to the Lord, to show that he was quenching his desire with the consolation of the word.

A sober mind, then, can rein in and repress the impulses of passions, however grievous, cool all the heat of the most burning desire, divert its motions elsewhere, and spit out the passions through the working of right reason. For when God established man and planted in him character and senses, he set over his impulses the royal rule of the mind, so that all of man's senses and impulses would be governed by its strength and power. As a further grace to his creature, he added that he would shape the mind itself with divine precepts and equip it with the teachings of wisdom, by which it might know what to avoid and recognize what to choose. The mind, therefore, holding fast through right reason to the teaching of wisdom, so as to know things divine and human, is instructed in the law, through which it learns which passions it ought to subject to itself.

The leaders, as it were, of the passions are the natural ones, pleasure and pain, and the rest follow them. For these two embrace all the others, and each of them is a passion not only of the body but also of the soul. And since we have said that other passions fall under these: before pleasure comes desire, after pleasure joy; before pain comes fear, after pain sorrow; while agitation of the mind is a passion common to both pleasure and pain. I will pass over the others, namely pride, avarice, ambition, contentiousness and envy, which are passions of the soul; I will pass over too the insatiable lust for gorging and the excesses of luxury and wantonness, vices bound up with the body and working through it. And it is rightly temperance above all that quenches the heat of these passions: first it tempers the soul with sobriety and moderation and shapes the mind, and then, by abstaining from delicacies, it draws tight the reins on the body's wildness. That is why the law cut back license in food and lavish feasting, not only to prune away luxury, but also so that, by reflecting on a restraining precept, it might open the way for the working of reason, which would cut back the enticements of the gullet and the other desires and hold in check the passions and impulses of the body. Temperance, then, is the forerunner of correction and the teacher of discipline.

Setting out from this, holy Jacob received from his brother the birthright he did not have, and, preferred over him with his own consent, taught for all time that the intemperate are worthless by their own judgment. Setting out from this, Joseph both tamed the heat of youth and strengthened his mind, when it was tempted by adulterous allurements, by bringing right reason to bear. For although he was strong and vigorous, he preferred to support himself by reasoning, saying to his master's wife: If, because of me, my master gives no thought to anything in his house, and has put all that he has into my hands, and nothing has been withheld from me except you, because you are his wife, how then shall I do this evil thing and sin before God? This, then, is the working of right reason, which the Greeks call logismos, by which the mind intent on wisdom is made firm. For it is a fine piece of reasoning: that he ought not to be ungrateful for his master's kindnesses, and that the sin could not be hidden, since he would be committing it with God as witness, from whom nothing can be concealed.

Reason, then, is good: it often strips away hostile feeling and puts aside the pain of injury. Indeed, in battle too it often softens the victor, holds back the sword of one about to strike, and snatches the suppliant from death, because just reason persuades him to spare the defeated. For on shutting out or softening the pain of injury, who is a better teacher than the patriarch Jacob, who rebuked his own sons Simeon and Levi, saying: You have made me hateful, so that I seem cruel. And yet they had avenged the wrong done to their sister, whose chastity had been violated and defiled against the customs of their fathers. Nor could Jacob, teacher of discipline and guardian of chastity, approve of the outrage committed; but he preferred that the insolent be restrained by reason, knowing that reason could temper indignation.

Temperance, then, is what cuts back desires. God commanded the first human beings to keep it, saying: But of the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of paradise you shall not eat, nor shall you touch it, lest you die. And because it was not kept, those who transgressed this outstanding virtue were made exiles from paradise and lost their share in immortality. This virtue the law teaches and pours into the hearts of all.

Scripture testifies that it can be taught, and wisdom and discipline as well: temperance in the law, and the others in the book of Job, where it is written: Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and discipline? And in the gospel the Lord himself says: Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart. And elsewhere he says to the disciples: Go, teach the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Why else were they called disciples, or what else did they learn from Christ but to carry out the precepts of the virtues? David too says: Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Certainly the fear of God is among the virtues, for the beginning of wisdom is the fear of God, through which the pattern of godly teaching is taken up, of which Paul says: But thanks be to God that, though you were slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart that pattern of teaching to which you were handed over, and having been set free from sin you have become slaves of righteousness. Teaching, then, is what enables us to attain righteousness. So righteousness can be acquired by learning. Let us then apply ourselves with zeal to the pattern of the gospel's teaching. Very little zeal is often taken for a great deal. For everything depends on zeal, through which obedience is brought into play; and to whichever side obedience leans, it adds either guilt or grace. This drew us to death in the first Adam; this called us to life in the second Adam.

There is no reason to blame our misery on anyone but our own will. No one is held guilty unless he has turned aside by his own will. What is forced on the unwilling carries no charge; the reproach for offenses, which we would shift onto others, attaches only to what is done willingly. Christ chooses volunteers for his soldiers; the devil buys at auction slaves who sell themselves willingly. He holds no one bound under the yoke of slavery unless that person has first sold himself to him for the coin of sins. Why do we accuse the flesh as if it were weak? Our members are weapons of unrighteousness and weapons of righteousness. You saw a poor man being wronged and you protected him: your members are weapons of piety, with which you defended the poor man from wrong. You saw someone in need and gave him gifts: with your right hand you have driven death from your breast. You saw a man being led to death and you rescued him, for it is written: Rescue the one who is being led to death; your members are weapons of righteousness if you did not let a man perish unjustly. You saw a woman, you chastened your body, you put your lusts to death, you turned away from the wanton eyes of the harlot and left them behind: your members are weapons of chastity. But if, on the contrary, your eye saw a woman so as to desire her, you opened a wound and drove a dart into your own body: your members are weapons of sin. You saw the property of orphans and drove them from their fathers' homes, you moved the boundary stones your fathers set: your members are weapons of iniquity.

It is our disposition, then, not the flesh, that is the author of guilt; the flesh is the servant of the will. So let our will not sell us. The apostle cries out: Do you not know that when you offer yourselves to someone as slaves to obey him, you are slaves of the one you obey, whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness? So if we serve either sin or righteousness, let us consider on which side the slavery is more bearable and the fruit richer. But what fruit can there be in death? For the wages of sin is death, and so there is no fruit in it, only the loss of honor, when we blush at what we have done. But to serve righteousness is freedom; for whoever was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; likewise whoever was called as a free man is Christ's slave. Both conditions are excellent: to be under Christ, under whom slavery is precious and freedom glorious. Precious slavery, because it was purchased at the price of such great blood; glorious freedom, because no slavery to guilt, no chains of sins bind it, no burdens of shameful deeds, no traffic in crimes consign it to the degrading bond of servitude.

Learn humility, O man; recognize the force of the apostle's teaching. If you call yourself a slave, you are a freedman; if you boast of being free, you are a slave. For the one who was redeemed as a slave has freedom, and for the one who was called as free it is good to recognize that he is Christ's slave, under whom slavery is safe and freedom secure. Who would claim that Paul was ignorant, even in matters of law? He knew how to distinguish between a freedman and a freeborn man, and so it was not carelessly but precisely that he said: For whoever was called in the Lord as a slave is a freedman of the Lord; likewise whoever was called as free is a slave of Christ. Truly we are all Christ's freedmen; no one is freeborn, for all were born into slavery. Why do you, in a slave's condition, take on the arrogance of freedom? Why do you lay claim to titles of nobility, you heir of slavery? Do you not know that the guilt of Adam and Eve consigned you to slavery? Do you not know that Christ redeemed you, not bought you? You were redeemed not with gold and silver from the empty way of life handed down by your fathers, but with the precious blood of the Lamb, cries the apostle Peter. So you have been redeemed by the Lord: you are a slave because you were created, a slave because you were redeemed, and you owe service to him both as master and as redeemer. Do not think that being a freedman under Christ is inferior to being freeborn. It is equal in dignity, superior in protection, equal in grace, more guarded against falling, better shielded against pride. You received freedom on the terms that you must remember the one who set you free, and know that lawful deference is owed to your patron, so that freedom may not be revoked from you as an ingrate. Who is more blessed than you, who reign under a master and serve as a soldier under a patron?

What is there that the Lord has not bestowed on you? He gave the law, and added grace. For the law made sin known, but in our slippery condition it could not wholly restrain it. I came to know sin, which I had not known; I came to know that concupiscence is sin, and on this occasion of knowing sin the debts piled up, because sin, which earlier seemed dead through my ignorance, came back to life in me; and I died under the wound of sin, because the knowledge of guilt, which seemed likely to benefit me, harmed me, in that I knew what I could not avoid. For it exposed sin, and by the good of its warning it heaped up the odium of sin itself. So sin became excessive for me, because it was heaped up by the declaration of the commandment; for guilt grows when it is exposed and not guarded against. How then is the commandment good, when it is death to me? Or how is it not death to me, when sin, in order to be shown up through the good of what the commandment signifies, has worked death in me? For it is certain that death came upon me when I recognize what I do as sin, as the Lord himself says: If I had not come and spoken to them, they would have no sin.

Why then are you surprised if the law brings death to some, when even the saving coming of the Lord, by which we were redeemed, brings death to some? For the unbeliever seeks death for himself from grace, yet the grace of the commandment remains. Just as knowledge of poisonous drinks serves to perfect the discipline of medicine, so the divine commandment serves for eternal life. But just as, for someone who misuses harmful potions, his knowledge of them turns to evil and danger, and the more he knows of poisons the more he realizes he is in peril, so the form of the commandment becomes the author of death for those who misinterpret the law, or who cannot avoid sins even once they have been pointed out and forbidden. So just as an antidote is good, even if it is not good for the imprudent or the intemperate, so the commandment is good, even if it is not good for the intemperate. Therefore the commandment which is death to someone is good. Here, then, is the answer to the first proposition: the commandment which is death to me can be good—good by the nature of a saving precept, death through the intemperance of the flesh.

And since we have learned that the commandment which is death to me is good, let us now examine how what has worked death in me, albeit through the good, is not death to me. For this is how the apostle put it: Did what is good, then, become death to me? By no means; but sin, so that it might be shown to be sin, worked death in me through what is good. So let us look at each point. The commandment, certainly, belongs to the law, and the law is spiritual: I see its grace, I praise its beauty, I proclaim its form, I admire its precept. But because I am carnal and sold under sin, I am dragged against my will into guilt; for guilt lords it over me as over a slave. So I hate the crime and commit it. The mind hates, the flesh desires; yet I am in both, I who with the mind consent to the law and with the flesh do what I do not want. Good, then, is the commandment to which I consent, and good is the mind that chooses what is good. It is good at judging, but often weak at resisting, because the appetite of the body fights against it and drags it captive into the allurements of error.

In this danger there is one remedy: that the grace of God should set free the one whom the law could not set free. For so it is written: Wretched man that I am, who will set me free from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. So it comes about that, although the sin that lay hidden—that is, my concupiscence, which I did not think was sin—worked death in me when it was exposed, and sin itself became excessive (for it was sin even when it was not known, but it was heaped up by knowledge and took on, as it were, an increase of error, and the form of the commandment passed over into the nature of an offense), yet it is not death to me, for I can readily take refuge in Christ, through whom we are released from every danger of death. The second proposition, then, is also resolved: the commandment of the law is not death to me, even if it works death. That we are troubled is due to our frailty; that we escape is due to Christ.

So, to return to the beginning of this discourse: the mind is good that has the working of reason and applies itself to the teachings of wisdom; but it has a heavy struggle with the body of death, and the allurement of the flesh often overcomes the reason of the mind. That is why the Lord first gave the law, to which the human mind gave itself in obedience and began to serve, so as to be subject to it; but the flesh was not subject, because the wisdom of the flesh is not subject to the law, and it fought against its precepts. For, given over to desires and entangled in carnal seductions, it could not obey virtue. Therefore we must strive to hold fast to the grace of God. The mind, then, is good if it is intent on reason, but far from perfect unless it has Christ at the helm. For the Lord Jesus came to nail our passions to his cross and to forgive sins. In his death we were justified, so that the whole world might be cleansed by his blood; indeed, it was into his death that we were baptized.

If, then, our sins are forgiven us in his death, let the passions of our sins also die in his death, and let them be held fast, fixed by the nails of his cross. If we have died in his death, why are we called back again, as though still alive, to the things of the world? What have we to do with the elements of the world, what with desires, what with luxury and wantonness, to which we died in Christ? But if we have died in Christ, we have risen in Christ; let us therefore live with Christ, and with Christ seek the things that are above, not things corruptible and earthly. Christ, rising from the dead, left the old man nailed to the cross and raised up the new. Christ died so that we too might die to sin and rise again to God. Our flesh is dead; why does it come back to life for sin, why does it obey sin again? Why does sin reign again among the dead, when death is the end of sin? We have died in the flesh; we have been renewed in the spirit. Let us walk in the spirit, for we have received the Spirit of Christ. And if Christ is in us, then let the flesh be dead to us because of sin, but let the spirit live because of justification.

In this way what was impossible for the law is accomplished, if we walk in the spirit; in this way we bury the passions, if we do not undo the cross of this body, if we do not write out again the bond of sin that was blotted out on the cross of Christ, if we do not put on again the garment of the old man which we have taken off. For it is written in the Song of Songs: I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them? The members of the body, then, have been put to death in us; why do its vices sprout again? The law did not prevail, because it did not put the flesh to death; it passed away like a shadow, because it gave no color; it even cast a shadow over us, blocking the sun of righteousness, because it heaped up crimes; and so it also did harm.
What need was there, then, for the law to be promulgated, if it was not going to be of benefit?

We already had the law of nature. Each person was a law to himself, having the work of the law written in his heart. We did not keep that law. Why, then, was a second one added, by whose works the flesh could not be justified? What came was a chain, not a release. What was added was knowledge of sins, not their forgiveness. We all sinned, we who could have pleaded ignorance as our excuse: every mouth has been stopped.

Yet it did me good. I began to confess what I used to deny. I began to recognize my offence and not to cover my injustice. I began to declare my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart. And this also benefits me, that we are not justified by the works of the law. So I have no ground for glorying in my own works, nothing to boast of in myself, and therefore I will glory in Christ. I will not glory because I am righteous, but because I have been redeemed. I will glory not because I am free of sins, but because my sins have been forgiven. I will not glory because I have done good or because anyone has done good to me, but because Christ is my advocate with the Father, because Christ's blood was shed for me. My guilt has become for me the price of redemption, and through it Christ came to me. For my sake Christ tasted death. Guilt has borne more fruit than innocence. Innocence had made me arrogant; guilt has made me humble.

You see, then, the ways in which the giving of the law has benefited you. But you say that through the law sin abounded. Yet where sin abounded, grace abounded too. You have died to sin, O man; so the law no longer harms you. You rise again through grace; so the law has done good, because it won grace. You have also received a pledge of Christ's love, since he who died for you is your advocate and keeps in store the reward of his blood. And he who reconciled the sinner to the Father commends the innocent much more, and protects the one who submits to him, because he has taken him as his own, free of guilt.

Do you, then, who owe so great a kindness, not repay it with obedience? He has made you an heir, he has made you a fellow heir: an heir of God, a fellow heir with Christ. He has poured into you the Spirit of adoption. Count these things up, and add them not so much to the bond of a debt as to the keeping of a gift received. You are a fellow heir with Christ if you suffer with Christ, if you die with him, if you are buried with him. Take up his sufferings, so that you may be found worthy to be with him beyond sufferings. See how he forgave your former sins, so that nothing you had done wrong could harm you. See how he urges you not to lose what you have received. The race of this labour is short, and the crown is fruit that lasts for ever; the suffering is bearable, the reward beyond price. What is it that troubles you? Is it the contempt shown to low birth? But in the age to come you will have a glorious nobility of devotion and faith. Is it a slender income, a meagre living? But you will have the riches of an eternal reward, in which you can lack nothing. Is it the loss of children? You will receive back for ever those whom you had received for a time. It will be said of you: “Blessed is he who has offspring in Zion and kinsfolk in Jerusalem.” “The sufferings of this time,” it says, “are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come”: so Scripture tells you.

Add that the blessed life is not diminished by these adversities, whether the troubles of this world or the sufferings of the body, but is rather proved by them. Add that it either does not feel the loss of an inheritance, or with a brave mind hides the loss of those dear to it and swallows its grief. Add that he who is always in the harbour of tranquillity knows nothing of shipwreck. And what of the fact that your labour is shared with all creation, that for your sake the world itself endures bondage to corruption, that you share in common with the saints a fellowship in this labour and in this waiting? The sun knows its setting, the moon its waning, the lights of the stars their wandering, while we await the redemption of our whole body.

But do you fear the uncertain twists and turns of life and the snares of the adversary, when you have God's help, and so great a regard from him that he did not spare his own Son for you? Scripture used a beautiful word to show the loving purpose of God the Father toward you, who offered his Son to death. The Son could not feel the bitterness of death, yet as far as it lay with the Father, he kept nothing back for himself but offered everything for you; for in the fullness of the godhead he himself lost nothing, and he redeemed you. Consider a father's love. As love would, he took on the danger as though his son were about to die; he drank the grief as though of bereavement, so that the fruit of redemption might not be lost to you. So eager was the Lord for your salvation that he all but put what was his own at risk in order to win you. For your sake he took on our losses, so as to graft you into divine things and consecrate you to heavenly ones. And he added, wonderfully: “He gave him up for us all,” to show that he loves all so much that he would give up his most beloved Son for each one. For those to whom he gave what is above all things, can it be that he has not given everything with him? He who gave up the author of all things held nothing back.

There is nothing, then, that we need fear may be refused us, nothing in which we ought to doubt the constancy of God's generosity, whose abundance has been so lasting and unbroken that first he predestined, then he called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified. Could he abandon those whom he has attended with such great kindnesses all the way to their reward? Among so many kindnesses of God, are we to fear any snares of the accuser? But who would dare accuse those whom he sees chosen by God's judgement? Can God the Father himself, who bestowed his gifts, revoke them, and banish from the grace of a father's love those whom he has taken up by adoption? But there is the fear that the judge may be too stern. Consider whom you have as judge. Surely the Father has given all judgement to Christ. Could he, then, condemn you, whom he redeemed from death, for whom he offered himself, whose life he knows to be the reward of his own death? Will he not say, “What profit is there in my blood, if I condemn the one I myself have saved?” Besides, you consider the judge but not the advocate. Can he pass too harsh a sentence who never ceases to intercede, so that the grace of reconciliation with the Father may be granted to us?
But even if grievous things were to threaten us, they ought in no way to separate us from Christ.

Why should we not endure even hard and bitter things for him, who for us underwent such unworthy treatment? So the love in us ought to be such that no dangers call us back from Christ. For it is written: “Much water cannot shut out love, and rivers will not enclose it,” because the soul of one who loves crosses the torrent. No storm, no deep danger, no terror of death or punishment lessens the strength of love. In these we are proved; in these the blessed life is found, even if it is flooded by many dangers.

For the wise man is not broken by pains of the body or troubled by hardships, but remains blessed even in afflictions. Bodily adversities neither diminish the gift of the blessed life nor take anything away from its sweetness, because the blessedness of life does not lie in the body's pleasure. It lies in a conscience pure from every stain of sin, and in the mind of one who knows that what is good gives delight even if it is harsh, while what is unseemly gives no comfort even if it is sweet. So the ground of living well is not bodily pleasure but the mind's wisdom. It is not the flesh, which is subject to passion, but the mind, which judges; for nothing delights more than honourable counsels and beautiful deeds. The mind, therefore, is the interpreter of the blessed life. For wisdom or reason, the judge of passion, is better than passion, and what judges is superior to what is subject to judgement. It cannot be that what is irrational is better than reason. So he who follows Jesus has his reward within himself, and in his own disposition his prize and grace. Even if he endures hard things, he is still blessed in his character, blessed in the very dangers, as the Lord laid down when he said: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake.”

There is, then, a blessed life among men, but only, of course, among those in whom life has been made perfect. The perfect life is not this life of the senses but that rational life which follows the working of reason and the liveliness of the mind. In this consists not a part of man but his perfection, which lies not so much in man's condition as in his activity; for it is this that makes him blessed. For such a man, then, what is the good but himself? What he has, this good, is present to him and will be the cause of good things to come. Of this good Solomon said: “Drink water from your own vessels and from the springs of your own wells. Let the waters of your own fountain overflow for you, and run through your own streets. Let them be set aside for you alone, and let no stranger share them with you. Let the fountain of your water be your own.”

Make use, then, of your inner good. The greatest evidence of this good is that one who has it seeks nothing else. For what would he seek who looks down on lesser things and clings to what is most excellent, as it is written: “Let the stag of friendship and the foal of graces converse with you”? Let friendship go before you and be with you at all times; for the friendship of the virtues is good, and so is the love of the highest good. So that perfect man seeks nothing else except the one and glorious good. Hence he also says: “One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life and see the delight of the Lord.” Do not scorn him as cramped and needy because he is content with the company, so to speak, of the one good alone. Surrounded by its friendship, he will be very rich. This is more than enough for such a man for blessedness and for possession of the good, and so he desires nothing else. One who has everything seeks nothing as if it were new. There is no good that he does not have. He takes no delight in superfluous things, only in necessary ones, and those necessary not for himself but for the flesh that clings to him. And he allows only what does not conflict with the purpose of the inner man, so as to make the two one and reconcile both the inner and the outer man to God, that in both there may be one spirit.

A man of this purpose, then, is not diminished by losses, not broken by adversities, not held back by obstacles, not saddened by the loss of those dear to him. To shape such a man the apostle says: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, about those who have fallen asleep, so that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.” For he comforts himself with faith in the resurrection and the grace of the reward to come. With the mind by which he clings to God he does not admit sorrow, and he rejoices in the delight of God's presence. One who is saddened by these things is not saddened according to God, and what is not according to God is full of folly. So the sorrow of this world, which is not according to God, is far from the perfect man, as is all anxiety over bodily affliction. In this kind of account of the mind and of its substance, the condition of the body and a certain outward use of nature are not counted. At the same time, an unconquered spirit must keep the same steadiness in the face of the body's pleasures and the very frailty of nature, of bereavements, losses and insults. So whoever desires to hold the palm of blessedness must cut himself off from the body itself and strip off the senses of the flesh; for its fruit lies not in the share of one virtue but in the fellowship of many, and if possible of all.

The perfect man, then, does not know or feel the troubles of this body or the adversities of the world, for he keeps his mind free of any fear that they may befall him. A life is not defined as more perfect if it lacks these things, but if it despises them. For if it were defined so that the blessed life was one found free and empty of such misfortunes, then certainly no one could be called blessed when they befell him. Therefore these things have been set aside, and only this was required in assessing the blessed life: that its definition should rest not on other things but on the possession of the true and the good, since one who has that spurns everything else and does not look for it.

Now I ask whether the wise man takes delight in the health of the body. We cannot deny that he takes delight in it according to nature, and would gladly rather feel no pain than feel it, except perhaps for Christ's sake. For Christ, if the cause demands it, he would readily accept weakness of body and offer his whole body to death. Yet even apart from the cause of faith and justice, if he lacks health, he is not troubled in mind or broken by bodily pain, for he can find comfort in the perfection of the virtues.

I ask also whether he takes delight in his children. Who would deny it? We are looking not for a hard man of iron but for a perfect one. Yet even if he loses his children, he is not on that account less blessed, since he is not less perfect; for what is perfect is blessed. Indeed, such a man is usually thought more perfect if he endures adversity than if he abounds in prosperity, although virtue usually loses or gains nothing whether outward advantages or bodily comforts are absent or present. Many have won as much praise for bravely enduring adversity as for not having met it. But these things are judged by appearance, not by weight.

This is the deep truth: that the just man wants nothing but that one and glorious good, gives his attention to it alone, counts it alone among good things, and always desires not something else along with it but it alone, and delights in it. If something else is added that delights him, such as the sweetness of children, the first is not lost but the second is added. Accidental things cannot diminish blessedness, since they cannot increase it; for that remains full and inviolable into which the soul has clothed itself, into which it has grafted and poured itself. Perfect virtue remains always the same amid both adversity and delight. Adversities take nothing from its perfection and delights add nothing to it. For how should one who has climbed to the summit feel either loss or gain from perishable things?

Nor will he think himself wretched, though most people consider this the heaviest blow, if either he or his children are taken into captivity; for he will not find unbearable what belongs to nature or what seems good to the Lord. Indeed, the just man said: “Good is the word which the Lord has spoken,” and he said: “Let there be peace and faithfulness in my days.” Surely the righteous Hezekiah was not glad that the misery of captivity had been turned aside onto his sons. But he could not oppose the Lord's will, and so he accepted his commands calmly, like a servant. Besides, he could reckon that the merit of virtue can shine out even in captivity. For Jeremiah was no less blessed in captivity, nor Daniel, nor Ezra, nor the blessed Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael, than if they had not fallen into captivity, since they were led into captivity precisely so that they might bring the people comfort in their present captivity and hope of escaping it. It is the mark of a perfect man to bear the common lot of nature with strength of mind and turn it to something better, and not to give way before things that seem terrible and frightening to most people. Like a brave soldier he withstands the onslaughts of the heaviest misfortunes and enters the fight; like a careful helmsman he steers the ship in a storm, and by meeting the rising waves he escapes shipwreck by cutting through the waves rather than by turning aside from them. Such a man is not fearful in persecution, nor softer under torture for fear of provoking the torturer. Like a strong athlete he strikes back at the one who beats him, if not with the lash of blows then certainly with the lash of words. He despises the tortures that many dread, saying: “Their wounds have become like the arrows of children.” Though he struggles with the heaviest pain, he does not show himself pitiable, but shows that, like a light in a lantern, the strength of his spirit shines even amid fierce storms and the heaviest blasts and cannot be put out. Such a man is not weak when wrongs are done to those dear to him, nor anxious about the burial of his own body, for he knows that heaven is owed to it. In the captivity of his people he is not cast down, but like a stern judge he condemns the treachery and errors of unbelievers, as Daniel did, who exposed the thefts of the priests and refuted their superstitions, showing that they rested on no truth but were shadowed over with frauds. Such, in short, is the perfect man: he wants everyone to do well and no harm to befall anyone, and if harm does befall against his will, he himself still loses nothing of his own blessedness.

But someone may think that sickness and weakness of body are a hindrance to fulfilling the task of perfection, because no work of the hands or deeds can then go forward. The just man, however, will not feel these things as a hindrance to himself. Indeed, he will rebuke the one who weeps over them pitifully and charge him with cowardice: for setting more store by the use of the body than by the virtue of the mind; for longing for things he should be master of, when he has the power rather to command others; for groaning in poverty when he could be above the riches of the world, since to the faithful the whole world is full of riches; for bewailing low birth when he ought to look down on royal powers and command the rich and mighty. For this is the life of the just man: he should regard whatever means he has as common property, and even divide them among the needy and distribute them to the poor. He should cut back his own pleasures, reduce his spending, practise the thrift of temperance, keep sober in prosperity, patient in adversity, enduring in pain, great-hearted in dangers. He should not know wishes for unbroken health, nor be shaken by the terror of approaching death. He should not think a man better because, according to nature, he has been blessed in abundance with children, relatives, health, joy and plenty, than one who has lacked them. He should weigh merits not by the outward goods of this world but by the inner goods of virtue.

Who would deny that this too is the pattern of the just man: that he fears nothing and dreads nothing except the loss of virtue, and that he checks the empty fears of others, which they have from anxiety about dangers, fear of death and weakness of body? He should teach that to depart from the body and be with Christ is far better, and show that good works are not hindered by bodily weakness but increased. He is commended not by the splendour of his family, the support of his relatives or his wealth, but by good disposition. For Elijah was no less blessed than Moses. The one, in need of food, in a cheap sheepskin, without children, without means, without companion; the other, leader of peoples, blessed with offspring, girded with power: in different ways they laid the foundation of equal merit. This was made plain in the gospel when they shone with the Lord Jesus in the glory of the resurrection; for he seems to have given them an equal reward, as equal witnesses of his glory. Nor was Elisha less blessed than David. The one was subject to kings, the other endowed with royal power, yet they obtained a grace of prophetic holiness not at all unequal.

What does he lack who possesses that good and always has virtue as his companion and partner? In what condition is he not most powerful? In what poverty is he not rich? In what lowliness of birth is he not illustrious? In what leisure is he not hard at work? In what weakness is he not vigorous? In what infirmity is he not strong? In what rest of sleep is he idle, whom his own virtue does not leave even while he rests? In what solitude is he not surrounded by a crowd, he whom the blessed life encircles, whom grace clothes, whom the mantle of glory makes bright? For he is no less blessed at leisure than when he works, and no less glorious asleep than awake, because he is no less safe and sound asleep than when he is awake. When can he be thought idle, whose mind is always at work? When is he alone, who is always with that good of which the prophet says, “We shall be filled with the good things of your house”? When is he cast down, whose citizenship is in heaven? When is he without beauty, who conforms himself to the likeness of that beauty and of the only good, who even if his limbs are failing still lifts himself up in mind? Think of one who used to play the lyre: if he sees it broken apart, its strings slack and its frame shattered, so that it can no longer be played, he throws it aside and no longer looks for its music, but soothes himself with his own voice. In the same way this man will let the lyre of his body lie idle and will delight himself in his heart. He will soothe himself with the memory of a good conscience and lift himself up with the divine oracles and the writings of the prophets. He holds in his soul and embraces in his mind that sweet and joyful good to which nothing sad can happen, since the grace of the divine presence always breathes upon him, and he himself is at peace with himself, steeped in the deepest tranquillity of spirit.
BOOK TWO.

In the previous book we discussed the precepts of the virtues. In this one let us use the examples of illustrious men who, though placed in the greatest dangers, did not lose the happiness of life but rather gained it. Was not blessed Jacob happy even when he left his homeland? Indeed he was plainly happy, for he took on the hardships of exile in order to calm his brother's anger. If a man who avoids sin is happy, then surely one who relieves another of guilt and turns him away from crime cannot be denied happiness. By a voluntary exile, then, he averted a murder that was already prepared, and by this act he secured his own safety and gave his brother the gift of innocence. Rightly, therefore, divine grace accompanied him everywhere, so that even while he slept he gained the gift of the happy life: for he saw the mysteries of things to come and heard divine oracles. He was a good worker even in his sleep and rich in his poverty, for by the service of a hired man's life he obtained both property and a wife through one and the same labour. He was also an excellent reconciler of brotherly affection, vying with gifts and courtesies to banish all resentment and to turn aside the pain of offence, showing that he had not been diminished by exile, since he could give away what he had not received.

But I am hurrying on too quickly to what follows and passing over useful matters, since we must first define what it is to be happy. For it is written: "Happy is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence." By this Scripture means that the happy man is one who has either kept himself from the company of the faithless (for this is ungodliness: not to acknowledge the author of life and, as it were, the parent of salvation), or has not remained in sin, or has not persisted in luxury and wantonness. It also says that the man who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night will be like a tree that will yield its fruit in its season. The former are the merits that earn rewards; this is the reward of merits.

Which of these things that pertain to the merits of happiness did holy Jacob lack? He kept so far from the company of the ungodly that the faithful people took its name from him, being called Israel, because he beheld God with the eyes of the inner mind. He abstained from sin and was sober, free from the drunkenness of all luxury, so that he swallowed hardships and toil and disregarded the comforts of leisure. Is it not beautifully and truly said of him too that he will yield his fruit in its season, of whom it is written: "See, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field"? For he was perfect in every flower of the virtues and gave off the fragrance of the grace of sacred blessing and heavenly happiness. He himself is the field which the Lord has blessed: not this earthly field, bristling with woods, or broken by torrents, or marshy with sluggish waters, or barren of grain, or useless for vines, or stony with still unfruitful gravel, or cracked and parched with drought, or soaked with blood, or wild with briars and thorns, but that field of which the Church says in the Song of Songs: "I have adjured you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field." For this is the field of which the Lord also says: "And the beauty of the field is with me." In this field is found that grape which, when pressed, poured out blood and washed the world clean; in this field is that fig tree under which the saints will rest, refreshed by the sweetness of spiritual grace; in this field is that fruitful olive tree that flows with the ointment of the Lord's peace; in this field bloom the pomegranates, which cover many fruits with the single defence of faith and cherish them in a kind of embrace of love.

These, then, were the fruits whose fragrance Jacob gave off, he who followed God through dangers and believed himself safe everywhere under his guidance. For although the smell of a field is sweet and pleasant, since it is the smell of nature, yet in the holy patriarch it was the grace of the virtues that breathed. How restrained he was in his frugality, for he did not desire the food prepared for himself but gave it without delay to his brother when he asked for it, and from him he received the primacy of the blessing! How dutiful toward his parents, so that he deserved by his mother's affection to be preferred to his elder brother and was consecrated by the gift of his father's blessing! How devout, in refusing to harm his brother! How modest, in fearing to deceive his father! How respectful, in being unable to refuse his mother what she commanded!

But we must not leave his parents unexcused for preferring the younger son to the elder. At the same time we must take care that no one, while looking to their example, judges unfairly between his children, thinking that one should be loved and the other set aside. For from this brotherly hatreds are stirred up, and over the increase of some paltry money the crime of murdering a kinsman is plotted. Let the same measure of affection cherish all one's offspring. Granted that affection may seize something more for the child who is more endearing or more like oneself, still the standard of justice ought to be the same toward all. More is given to the favoured child when the love of his brothers is sought for him; but more is taken from the one who is burdened with the envy that unjust preference brings. Esau threatened to kill his brother, and neither brotherhood nor reverence for his parents called him back from his murderous fury; he was grieved that the blessing had been snatched from him, though he ought to have proved himself worthy of it by gentleness, not by crime.

But Rebekah too preferred not one son to another son, but the righteous to the unrighteous. For with a devout mother the mystery outweighed her child: she was not so much preferring him to his brother as offering him to the Lord, knowing that he could keep the gift bestowed on him. In this she was also looking out for the other, whom she was withdrawing from God's displeasure, so that he would not be entangled in heavier guilt if he lost the grace of a blessing once received.
Consider, however, a good contest between parents. Let the mother bestow affection, the father judgment.

Let the mother lean toward the younger with tender love; let the father preserve for the elder the honour that is his by nature. Let him honour more, let her love more. While each cherishes one, let them not both conspire toward one and defraud the other. Let there be equality amid their different rivalries, and by their unlike preferences let equal favour be bestowed on both through the equal love of the parents. Let the one make up for what the other lessens. In this way, with devoted affection, the patriarch Isaac and holy Rebekah vied with each other so as to make neither son inferior, but both equal.

Yet he won who was preferred by the oracle: diligence won over slowness, gentleness over harshness. While the other sought wild game in the rough hunt, this one served his devout father the food of gentle manners, the grace of home, the sweet dishes of tender gentleness and devotion. Whatever comes to hand naturally pleases minds more than anything you think must be offered with contrivance. Jacob went to the sheep and brought the offspring of innocence, or rather the gifts of sacred prophecy, because he believed that no food was sweeter to the patriarch than Christ, who was led like a sheep to the slaughter and like a lamb to the sacrifice. This he judged to be wholesome food both for the father of the nation and for the people whose type he bore, since by it the forgiveness of sins was to come.

He received his brother's robe because he excelled in the wisdom of age; the younger brother stripped the elder because he shone forth in the dignity of faith. Rebekah, as a type of the Church, brought out this robe and gave it to the younger son: the robe of the Old Testament, the prophetic and priestly robe, that royal robe of David, the robe of Solomon, of the kings Hezekiah and Josiah. And she gave it to the Christian people, who would know how to use the garment they received, since the Jewish people kept it without using it and did not recognize their own adornments. This robe lay in the shadow, cast aside and neglected; for it was darkened by the gloomy fog of ungodliness and could not be unfolded more broadly in the narrow heart of that people. The Christian people put it on, and it shone. They lit it up with the brightness of their faith and the light of godly deeds. Isaac recognized the familiar smell of his own race, he recognized the robe of the ancient Scripture, but he did not recognize the voice of the ancient people, and so he knew that it had been changed. For the same robe remains even today, but the confession of a more devout people has begun to ring out, and rightly he said: "The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau." And he smelled the smell of his garments. And perhaps the meaning is this: we are justified not by works but by faith, because the weakness of the flesh is a hindrance to works, but the brightness of faith, which merits the pardon of sins, overshadows the error of our deeds.

After the blessing had been given, the elder brother arrived. This shows that the kingdom was bestowed on the Church in predestination before the synagogue, but that the synagogue came in so that sin might abound, and when sin had abounded, grace might also abound. At the same time it makes clear that the candidate for the heavenly kingdom must be eager, so as to snatch the blessing and claim the privilege of being commended. Hence the younger son was not rebuked by his father but praised, for Isaac said: "Your brother came with guile and took your blessing." Guile is good where the seizing is blameless; and the seizing of devotion is blameless, because from the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force. So too the fathers celebrated the Passover in haste, eating the lamb hurriedly and without delay; and holy Joseph, by the device of a pious deception, summoned his brother Benjamin and kept him.

Yet Esau too, by pressing, drew out and obtained a blessing for himself, but a blessing that fitted and agreed with the former one: that he should serve his brother. For one who could not command and govern another ought to serve, so as to be governed by one wiser. It was not the holy patriarch's intent to consign his son to the degrading condition of slavery; rather, as a good father who had two sons, one intemperate and the other prudent and sober, he looked to the good of both by setting the sober over the intemperate and ordering the foolish to obey the prudent. For the foolish man cannot be a willing disciple of virtue or persevere in its pursuit, since the fool changes like the moon. Rightly, then, he denied him the freedom of his own choice, so that he would not drift like a ship in the waves without a helmsman, but placed him under his brother, as it is written: "The foolish serves the wise." Rightly therefore he subjected him, so that under the rule of one who governed him he might improve his disposition. And so he said: "By your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother." For devotion is mistress over cruelty, and gentleness surpasses harsh impulses.

Everyone is a slave who lacks the authority of a pure conscience; whoever is broken by fear, or ensnared by pleasure, or led by desires, or provoked by indignation, or cast down by grief, is a slave. For every passion is servile, since whoever commits sin is a slave of sin, and, what is worse, one who is subject to vices is the slave of many. He has bound himself over to many masters, so that he can scarcely get free of his servitude. But the man who is master of his own will, judge of his counsel, interpreter of his choice, who restrains the craving of bodily passion, who does well whatever he does (and one who does well does rightly, and one who does rightly does so blamelessly and beyond reproach, having control of his own actions)—he is truly free. For only the one who does everything wisely and as he wishes is free. It is not a condition of fortune that makes a slave, but shameful folly. Indeed, a wise servant rules foolish masters, and their own slaves will lend to their masters. What will they lend? Not money, of course, but wisdom, as the law also says: "You shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow." The Jew lent the oracles of the divine law to the proselyte; but because he himself could not see the mysteries of the law and did not understand the oracles he possessed, he who once lent the letter to the Gentiles now borrows from them the grace of spiritual teaching. And rightly he has been made subject to servitude, since one who borrows is a slave, as though bound over to his creditor's interest, while one who imparts the interest of godly teaching is a prince, as the law says: "You shall be prince of many nations, but they shall have no princes over you." For the prince is the one who rules and holds the principality of wisdom. The Jewish people held it, but since they could not keep what they taught, they must now learn what they did not know how to teach.

This, then, is what the patriarch Isaac said: "You shall serve your brother. But it shall come to pass, when you put down and loosen his yoke from your neck." He was indicating that there would be two peoples, one the son of the slave woman, the other of the free woman—for the letter is a slave, grace is free—and that the people who hold to the letter would remain a slave until they followed the interpreter of spiritual teaching. Then also what the apostle says would come to pass: "that a remnant may be saved according to the election of grace." You shall serve your brother, then, but you will feel the benefit of servitude when you begin to obey your brother willingly rather than under compulsion.

From this envy arose, and Esau threatened to kill his brother after their father's death. But if such a thing should happen, let us learn from Rebekah how we must take precautions so that envy does not stir up anger and anger rush into the murder of a brother. Let Rebekah come—that is, let patience, the good guardian of innocence, be put on—and let her persuade us to give place to wrath. Let us withdraw somewhat farther off, until indignation softens with time and forgetfulness of the offence steals in. So patience does not dread even exile, but undertakes it readily, not so much to avoid danger to one's life as to avoid giving an incitement to crime. The devoted mother, too, bears the absence of her dearest son, meaning to do more for the one she had injured, yet looking out for both, so as to keep the one free from fratricide and the other untouched by crime.

We have heard what intemperance, drunk with bodily desires, has said; let us consider what true virtue does. It seeks nothing but the grace of God; it follows that one supreme good alone and is content with him alone, from whom we receive all things, while we ourselves give him nothing, because he needs nothing. As David says: "I said to my Lord: You are my Lord, for you have no need of my goods." For what does he need who abounds in all things, bestows everything on us, and supplies all things without ever running short?
And Jacob set out and slept, which is a sign of a quiet mind, and [?]
He saw the angels of God ascending and descending. That is, he foresaw Christ on earth, to whom the host of angels descends and ascends, ready to offer its own Lord the homage of devoted service.

And he came to a well, so that he might drink from his own vessels and from the springs of his own wells, and that waters might overflow for him from his own spring; for the fountain of life is in the hands of the just.

And he came to Laban and tended his sheep. Iniquity stays behind, unaccompanied; wisdom does not neglect its task of ruling. It cannot be idle even among strangers; it cannot be an exile among foreigners. For how could it be [?], when it keeps its own rights everywhere and holds within itself what it possesses?

The just man enters as a hired servant, yet he is the ruler, for by the ministry of gospel preaching he was gathering for himself a flock that shone with the splendour of many excellent virtues. So, for the sheep about to drink, he set rods of storax, of walnut and of plane in the channels, so that, longing for the mysteries of the most blessed Trinity prefigured there, they might form offspring by no means discoloured through the conception of a devout mind. Good sheep, which have brought forth offspring of good works not unworthy of the sacred faith! Storax signifies the incense and the evening sacrifice which is offered to God the Father in the psalm. By the walnut rod the priestly office is offered to Christ; for this is the rod of Aaron, which blossomed when it was laid up, and through which the priestly grace of sanctification shone forth. The plane tree signifies the abundance of spiritual fruit, because the vine is joined to this tree, so that in glad partnership with it the vine pours itself out in rich yield; for the gifts of the Lord's passion, together with the grace of the Spirit, are wont to foster the forgiveness of all sins.

By these means, as Scripture says, he became very rich, rearing a very good flock for Christ, which he ennobled with the title of faith and the variety of the virtues, the marks of a glorious name. So, rich in the wealth of faith, he did not think himself poor, and to Laban's sons he became an object of envy as a very wealthy man, since he had increased his own flock by adding to it another's. And God said to him: Return to the land of your father and to your own people, and I will be with you. He was showing that nothing was lacking to one who had the fullness of all things at hand; that for the perfect man this alone suffices in abundance, that in this all things hold together and all things are referred to him; that nothing was new to him, nothing superfluous, nothing necessary [?] lacking, since he had a sure peace through which he might reconcile things that had at first been at odds. Nor is it surprising that he had peace, who had set up a pillar and anointed it for God, which is the Church. For it is called the pillar and foundation of the truth. He anoints it who pours out the ointment of faith upon Christ and the ointment of mercy upon the poor.

Now let us consider what the just man ought to be like if envy has arisen. First, he should avoid it; for it is better to go away without strife than to stay on amid quarrelling. Next, he should possess only such things as he can take away with him, so that he cannot be held liable by his adversary in anything, but may say: See whether anything of yours is with me. And Laban searched and found nothing of his with Jacob. A great man and truly blessed, who could lose nothing of his own and had nothing of another's, that is, had nothing too little and nothing too much! So he is perfect who lacks nothing, and just who has nothing in excess; for this is to keep the measure of justice. How great was the virtue of one whose partnership brought gain and imposed no loss! This is what it is to be perfect: to give the greatest advantage to those who cling to you and to bring them no disadvantage.

Finally, the man who longed to harm him could not send him away empty. For the wise man is never empty, since he always has within himself the cloak of prudence; he can say, as Job said: I put on justice and clothed myself with judgment. For these are the inner garments of the mind, which no one else can take away, unless a man's own fault strips him. So it was that Adam, stripped in this way, was found naked; but Joseph, even when he had cast off his outer garment, was not naked, for he kept the garments of virtue intact. The wise man, then, is never empty. For how can he be empty who has received from the fullness of Christ and keeps what he has received? How can he be empty whose soul is full, guarding the garments of the grace it has received? What must be feared is that someone should lose the covering of innocence, that the ungodly, overstepping the bounds of justice in the assault of a sacrilegious persecution, should snatch away the garment of the soul and mind. This does not easily happen unless the voice of a man's own iniquity has first stripped him. Hence David too says: If there is iniquity in my hands, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies; let the enemy pursue my soul and seize it.

No enemy, then, can seize your soul unless it has first been made empty. So do not fear those who can plunder treasures of gold and silver. They take nothing from you. For they take what you did not truly have; they take what you could not possess; they take what did not adorn your soul but burdened it; they take what did not enrich your heart but rather weighed it down. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also, as you heard read today. Many lock up their gold behind the bolts of their doors, yet they do not trust even their bars and locks; many employ watchmen, yet they too are usually more afraid of the guards themselves; many brood over buried gold: their gold is under the earth, and their heart is under the earth. Take care, then, that you do not bury your own heart alive in the earth. So it is not thieves of that gold who are to be feared; the one you must beware of is that moneylender who scrutinizes the substance of your soul to see whether you have contracted any debt of graver sin, who shuts your heart up in the ground, who buries your soul under the same turf with which you have covered your gold, who bows your mind down under crushing interest and lays it in a heavy tomb from which no one rises again. Follow holy Jacob, who had nothing of other people's vices and was not empty and void of his own virtues, but was filled with the fruit of justice.

But these are moral lessons. The mystical sense is that Laban, that is, 'the whitened one', came to him, for Satan too transforms himself into an angel of light, and he began to demand his own things from him. Jacob answered him: See whether anything of yours is with me; that is: I have nothing of yours. Search, and see whether you recognize any of your vices and crimes. I have taken none of your frauds with me, I have no fellowship with your deceit; I have fled from everything of yours as from a contagion. And Laban searched and found nothing of his own. How blessed is the man in whom the enemy found nothing he could call his own, in whom the devil came upon nothing he could recognize as his! This seemed impossible in a man, but he bore the type of the one who said in the Gospel: The prince of this world will come and will find nothing in me. For whatever belongs to the devil is nothing, since it can have no permanence and no substance.

Now the one prefigured in Jacob is the Lord Jesus, the husband of two marriages, that is, one who shares as it were in both the law and grace. He first loved the virgin Rachel and cherished her with devoted affection as the one destined to be his bride. But since Leah, like the law, came in alongside, and crept in, weaker of eye, like the synagogue, which in the blindness of its mind could not see Christ, the grace of holy Rachel abounded all the more. She was sought in marriage beyond that first union, and even then by the meaning of her name she signified the future primacy of the Church. Blessed Rachel, who took away reproach by her childbearing! Blessed Rachel, who hid away the worship and errors of the Gentiles and showed that their idols were full of uncleanness! Let no one think that the reverence due to a father was violated because she remained seated while her father stood, for it is written: Whoever values father or mother more than me is not worthy of me. Where the cause of religion was at stake, faith had to occupy the judgment seat, and faithlessness had to stand like one accused.
These things were so approved that, as holy Jacob set out, the angels of God came to meet him.

Then he saw the camp of God drawing near and said: This is the camp of God; for divine protection is wont to be present to the perfect and the faithful. And being perfect, he was thinking about reconciliation with his brother, intending to win him over by humility, to gain him by kind services, and even to think of buying him with gifts. So he went to meet his brother with his wives and children, so that, even if Esau were angry with him, he might be softened by the dutiful attentions of kinship.

And he bowed down seven times to the ground. What does this mean? The law says: You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone; yet here he bows down to a man who was intemperate, wrathful, and threatening the crime of murdering his brother. Or did he worship the earth, that earth clotted with human blood, soaked with the venom of serpents, or wretched with barren gravel, or bristling with hard and rugged rocks? And what does it mean that he bowed down seven times? We would be at a loss for an explanation, were it not for what we find in the Gospel: when Peter asked, If my brother sins against me, how often shall I forgive him? Up to seven times? the Lord Jesus answered: Not only seven times, but seventy times seven. This, then, is what the holy patriarch signifies by the prophetic Spirit, looking ahead to the one who was to come and who would command that pardon be granted to a brother not only up to seven times but up to seventy times seven, so that Esau, approached with him in view, might forgive his brother the wrong he thought he had suffered and, though injured, might be restored to friendship. For this was why the Lord Jesus was to take flesh and come to earth: to grant us manifold pardon for our sins.

Then, as he was about to seek concord with his brother, he slept in the camp. Perfect virtue possesses the tranquillity and stability of rest; that is why the Lord reserved this gift of his for the more perfect, saying: My peace I leave with you, my peace I give to you. For it belongs to the perfect not to be easily moved by worldly things, not to be troubled by fear, not to be harried by suspicion, not to be shaken by terror, not to be tormented by grief, but, as on a perfectly safe shore, to keep the mind calm and unmoved at its secure anchorage against the rising waves of this world's storms. This firm foundation Christ brought to Christian minds, bringing inner peace to the souls of the approved, so that our heart may not be troubled nor our spirit harried. The apostle and teacher declared that this peace is above every mind, saying: And the peace of God, which surpasses every mind, will guard your hearts and thoughts in Christ Jesus. So the fruit of peace is to be undisturbed in one's heart. Indeed, the life of the just man is quiet, but the unjust man is full of restlessness and disturbance. And so the ungodly man is afflicted more by his own suspicions than most people are by the blows of others, and the weals of his wounds are greater in his soul than in the bodies of those who are beaten by others.

It is a great thing for someone to be tranquil within himself and to be at one with himself. Outward peace is sought either through the anxious foresight of an emperor or by the hand of soldiers, or it comes from the favourable outcome of wars, or from some slaughter of the barbarians when, stirred by hostility, they turn their weapons against themselves. In that peace there is no virtue of ours, but only chance. Certainly the glory of that peace is credited to the emperor, but the fruit of this peace, which is in our minds and held fast in the affections of each person, lies within us. The fruit of this peace is greater, since by it the temptations of spiritual wickedness are repelled, rather than the weapons of enemies. This peace, which shuts out the allurements of bodily passions and calms their disturbances, is loftier than the peace that checks the incursions of barbarians; for it is a greater thing to resist an enemy shut up within you than one far away.

So Jacob, who had cleansed his heart of all rancour and bore a peaceable disposition, after he had sent away all that was his, remained alone and wrestled with God. For whoever disregards worldly things comes nearer to the image and likeness of God. What is it to wrestle with God, if not to take up the contest of virtue, to grapple with one who is stronger, and to become an imitator of God greater than others? And because his faith and devotion were unconquerable, the Lord revealed hidden mysteries to him by touching the broad part of his thigh, because from his line the Lord Jesus was to spring, born of a virgin, who would be neither unequal nor unlike to God. The broad part of the numbed thigh signified his cross, because, by the forgiveness of sin spread through the whole world, it would bring salvation to all, and because by the numbness and sleep of his own body he would grant resurrection to the dead. Hence, not without reason, the sun rose upon holy Jacob, upon whose descendants the saving cross of the Lord shone; and also because the sun of justice rises for the one who sees God, since he himself is the eternal light.

And Jacob limped on his thigh. For this reason the children of Israel do not eat the sinew to this day. Would that they had eaten it and believed! But because they were not going to do the will of God, they did not eat it. There are also those who interpret it this way: that Jacob limped on one thigh because, of the two peoples springing from his line, the numbness of one with respect to the grace of faith was already being declared as soon to come. That, then, is the people that limped through the numbness of faithlessness.

Then, not long after a revelation of this kind, when Dina, Jacob's daughter, had been violated by the son of a foreigner and the modesty of her virginity defiled, her brothers, who did not understand the mystery, in their eagerness for revenge slew the foreigners, who were offering fellowship in the faith through a union of their peoples. But Jacob, who in his moral gentleness loved clemency, or else in the mystical Spirit foresaw the sacrament of the Church to be gathered from the Gentiles, received the spectacle of that vengeance unwillingly and with grief. Therefore, as he prophesied the coming of the Lord Jesus, a divine answer was given him: Arise, go up to the place Bethel, that is, to the house of bread, where Christ was born, as the prophet Micah testifies, saying: And you, Bethlehem, house of Ephrathah, are not the least, so as to be among the princes of Judah. For from you shall come forth a prince in Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of the ages. Truly a house of bread, which is the house of Christ, who came to us from heaven as the bread of salvation, so that no one may hunger any longer once he obtains for himself the food of immortality. There the patriarch is commanded to dwell, there to make an altar to God who appeared to him. There he received the foreign gods and hid them under a mastic tree; there, too, Rachel was buried, on the road, it says, to Ephrathah; this is Bethlehem. There also Jacob set up a pillar over her tomb.
What great mysteries! For there is the Church of God, in which God appears and speaks with his humble servants!

There the idols of the nations are taken away and hidden; for the faith of the Church has abolished every observance of paganism. But I ask why he hid them under a mastic tree. Certainly that kind of tree is unfruitful. The gods of the nations, then, are where there is no fruit. There the earrings of the Gentiles, which they gave to Jacob, are buried, so that they may now grow used to hearing a new language and forget the old sound [?] of faithlessness, so that their ears may become deaf to sacrilege and be cleansed for grace. Not without reason did holy Daniel there detect the false testimony against Susanna. For there faithlessness still wanted to plant its roots, but it could not stay hidden, since it was detected by the prophetic Spirit. And the error of the elder was fitting [?] to the true confession, in that he claimed chastity had been defiled in the very place where the idols of the nations are buried; but the truth of the Church did not shelter faithlessness: it buried it away and stopped the ears of paganism.

Fittingly, too, holy Rachel was buried there, because all who are baptized in Christ are buried together with him. For so we are taught by the apostle, who says: For we have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as he rose from death, raised by his own power, so we too may rise again by his grace. So all the error of the Gentiles is truly hidden away when someone has been washed clean of vices, because our old self, nailed to the cross, no longer knows how to serve the old sin. Fittingly, too, a pillar is set up over Rachel's tomb, because the Church is the pillar and foundation of the truth.

Now Jacob grew old, and he had already grown old in character before, but in him the unflagging vigour of youth vied with the tranquillity of old age. For there is an old age that is green with grace and a youth that is grey with wisdom, of which Scripture says: For venerable old age, and the age of old age, is a spotless life. Of this life was Jacob, who by good works anticipated the time of a long old age, so that he might both gather its fruit before its time and not fear its last days when they came. Blessed indeed is the young man who lives well, but blessed too is the old man who has lived well. For what the young man hopes for, the old man has obtained; what the old man has been, the young man wishes to be. Certainly the young man is still tossed by the waves of a restless sea, with a longer voyage still before him, while the old man rests in the anchorage of old age as in a harbour. Such, then, was Jacob, who held, already locked and sealed with the safe and secure key of grace, blessings that the young can scarcely hope for. And what you possess is better than what you still hope for. So Jacob was an old man to whom the young, struck by the storm of some adverse time, would betake themselves as into a harbour, while he himself, set as it were on a watchtower of this life, kept anxious and caring watch, and long beforehand foresaw remedies for uncertain affairs.
Then there was famine in all the land: the old man, laid aside [?], was the first to hear [?] what the eager young men did not know.

… [?] see. Meanwhile, he was the first to point out to his sons that grain was plentiful in Egypt, and that they must set out there to buy what they needed to live. He even agreed willingly to the young men's advice that he should send his younger son along with them. And when they brought back word that his son Joseph was alive, he did not wait for his son to come to him, though his body was broken; with the lively strength of his spirit he went to his son instead, for in matters of love the proper order of rank does not weigh most. So he felt none of the hindrances of weary old age as he travelled, because love lightened the labour.
