Then, having enjoyed the fruit of recovering his son for some time, namely seventeen years, which by the measure of a patriarch's long life is a small portion, he knew that the end of his life was drawing near. He called his son Joseph and bound him by an oath, through the future heir of his line, not to bury him in Egypt. Having received his pledge, when a little later he fell ill and his son Joseph came to him, he seemed to recover his strength: he sat up on his bed, blessed the twelve patriarchs, and prophesied.

Now let some say that blessed Jacob was not blessed when he was in his very last days, he who held converse with God almost more than with men; that he was not blessed when his eyes were heavy with age and he could not see. For to some people blindness seems a heavy and calamitous affliction. But even then Jacob was blessed, because he could distinguish in the spirit those whom he could not distinguish with his eyes and his sight. He who was thought not to see the present saw the future. Indeed, it was Joseph himself who was mistaken. He had placed his elder son at Jacob's right hand and his younger son at his left, so that the order of age might keep the order of the blessing; but Jacob stretched out his right hand over the younger grandson and his left over the elder. And when his son tried to move his father's right hand over to Manasseh, the elder, he answered: "I know, my son, I know. This one too shall become a people, and this one too shall be exalted; but his younger brother shall be greater than he." And he added the reason for the preference, saying: "His seed shall become a multitude of nations." So much better did he see, though the sight of his body was impaired, that he could teach the one who could see that he was mistaken. For who sees better than the one who sees Christ? Or who can call him hindered in his eyes who saw the Church shining forth in Christ? Is it not clear, then, that weakness cannot stand in the way of blessedness? He was deprived of the gift of his eyes, his bodily strength was worn out; yet leaving his body on the bed as though in a tomb, he rose up within himself, and gathering himself together far from others and deep within, he had withdrawn from present things and was mingling with the age to come in the last days. For so it is written: "I will tell you," he says, "what shall befall you in the last days."

What, then, did he lack, when God was with him, who had said to him as he set out: "I will go down with you into Egypt, and I will lead you forever"? Nor was God absent when the Holy Spirit was speaking in him. Who is as powerful in his own home as he was in a foreign one? Who is as rich in plenty as he was in famine? Who is as strong in youth as he was in old age? Who is as active in business as he was at rest? Who is as swift on the racecourse as he was on his bed? Who is as glad in the flower of youth as he was on the border of death? Who is as rich in a kingdom as he was in a foreign land? Indeed, he blessed kings. And rightly he was not poor, for he lacked nothing. He was not poor, for he did not think himself poor. And who would call him poor of whose company the world was not worthy, and whose citizenship was therefore in heaven? He was truly very rich in the riches of simplicity and sincerity, comely with a beauty of soul greater than that of body, a beauty that knows no fading; tireless in his age, able whenever he wished to leave this hovel of the body and to enter the heights of paradise by the vigour of his mind; rejoicing in spirit even as he gave his final instructions about his tomb. For he did not expect to be shut up in an earthly grave but to be received into a heavenly dwelling. And so he gave instructions about the tomb as if for someone else, while, untroubled about himself, he regarded that death as immortality. He seemed entangled in the encumbrance of the body, yet with watchful affection he ran ahead into times to come, speaking of the persecutors of the Lord, the authors of wickedness who were to come forth from the tribes of Simeon and Levi: "Let my soul not come into their council, and let my heart not hasten to meet them." And who is as mighty in strength as he was strong in weakness, when he said: "Cursed be their fury, for it was proud and reckless, and their wrath, for it was hardened. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel"?

Who is as melodious in song as he was in his words, which were heard by the whole world, and are heard among all peoples and in every age? Who, sweet in his measures, has sounded the differences of the seven notes as he resounded with the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit? Though his limbs were failing, he lifted himself up in mind and raised himself in spirit. The harmony of his body, like that of a lyre, was destroyed as the frame of his limbs came apart; but looking down on it from the height of his mind he did not seek it, and let it lie idle on the ground, while he soothed himself with an inner song and delighted in prophetic melody, saying: "Judah, your brothers shall praise you. Your hands shall be on the back of your enemies; your father's sons shall bow down to you. Judah is a lion's whelp; from the shoot you have gone up, my son. Lying down, you slept like a lion and like a lion's whelp. Who shall rouse him?" And further on: "He shall wash his robe in wine and his cloak in the blood of the grape. His eyes are merry with wine, and his teeth whiter than milk." What song is sweeter, what sound more pleasing, than the forgiveness of sins and the resurrection of the dead? This is the song that holy David, the instrument of the divine voice and interpreter of the Lord's word, sang on the spiritual lyre. With these strains of grace he soothed his lofty soul and mind. With this song he calmed the harshness of this world, with this sound he softened the hardships of this age, with this psaltery he broke the terror of death, with this sweetness of strings he trod the underworld underfoot.

But let us also hear the other things that the holy patriarch Jacob sounded forth on that wonderful instrument of his mind: "Naphtali is a vine let loose, putting forth beauty in its shoot. Joseph my son is increased, my son is increased, my son is envied, my youngest son; return to me." And further on: "He has prevailed over the blessings of the abiding mountains and the desires of the everlasting hills." What is sweeter than blessing, what more pleasing than eternity? The very words are a song, and in the words lie the great rewards of our prayers and the highest heights of merit.
What is sweeter than holy Joseph, who set us free from reproach through the mystery of the Lord's cross?

Christ became a curse to undo the curse of the law, and he became sin to take away the sin of the world. In the same way he became a reproach to remove the reproach of the Gentiles. But that reproach of Christ was valued above the treasures of Egypt. That is why Moses left the court of King Pharaoh and chose the reproach of faith, and for the sake of that reproach the seas divided before him. He, then, is Naphtali, a vine let loose through the whole world to pour the richness of the spiritual cup into every people. He is the one who is enlarged, having the name above every name. Because he offered himself to death for all, he hears from the Father: "Return to me." Jacob was speaking, but it was God who was heard. Jacob gave the blessing, but the Lord's voice rang out, saying to the Son: "Return to me." That is, return after the passion. Return to your throne, return with the trophy, return to me, so that the dead may follow you as you rise again, and by your power and your example may rise as well; so that you may become the firstborn from the dead and sit at the right hand of the Father. That is why the Son also said: "From now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of power."

Who would deny that blessed Jacob was blessed at the very last moment of death, when he poured out divine oracles? Who would deny that Joseph was blessed in prison, where by the spirit of wisdom he interpreted the truth of the dreams he had heard and revealed the course of things to come? Who would deny that Isaiah was blessed when he was sawn in two, or Jeremiah when he was sunk in the pit, or holy Daniel when he stood unafraid among the lions and a prophet, carried there by an angel, brought him his dinner? He was certainly not blessed because he was eating someone else's dinner, but because by his merits he shut the hungry mouths of the lions. And who would not call blessed the mother of the Maccabees? To the deaths of her seven sons she added herself as the eighth, for the glory of a heavenly triumph.

Nor will I pass you over, Eleazar. I am a priest speaking of a priest, but I am the one who needs the help of your prayers. You were a priest by descent, learned in the law and ripe in years. When you were brought before Antiochus the persecutor, you could not be caught by temptations, swayed by rewards or broken by bitter tortures. He began with flattery, since he thought his tortures might be overcome. "I feel shame before your grey hair," he said. "I revere your old age and admire your good sense. Why do you think you must refuse good food that nature freely gives? Give up this kind of obstinacy and wake up at last, while I still prefer persuading you to forcing you. Otherwise torture may defeat you, and you will do what you now refuse when reason invites you." The old man replied: "We are not driven by obstinacy, Antiochus. We are bound by reverence for the law, which commanded us to abstain from pork. You judge the pig a most beautiful creature, yet you cannot deny that self-control is better than pleasure, and obeying the law better than breaking it. If you think eating pork a trivial matter, how will someone who despises the law in the smallest things keep it in great ones? Or if such a creature is precious, you are avenged when we are deprived of something so beautiful. Our abstinence is a training in chastity. Through it we learn to cut back luxury, conquer our desires, shut out lust and resist the pleasures of the body. It is also an exercise in courage not to give way to punishment for the sake of the law. It is a mark of justice and of prudence too, that what we chose to follow out of fear of God we keep even when death is set before us. Who would dictate to free men what they eat? And who would make himself a laughingstock by becoming a slave in this? But you will not laugh. I am not so old that the courage of my spirit cannot grow young again."

So he was strung up and beaten hard from one side and then the other. When his old limbs could no longer bear the punishment of the blows, and the executioners and those who stretched him were worn out, he sank to the ground, but his mind would not bend. Then someone spoke to him, either out of pity for his great age or wanting to trap him by temptation: "Just say that you will eat. We will make sure you are spared that food." But he cried out: "Never let it happen that I, an old man, should lead the young into error, when until now I have been a model of a wholesome way of life. Shall I win a little more life through this charade, and sign away the labours of my whole life for the brief provisions of old age? Old age should be a harbour, not the shipwreck of the life that came before. I will not deny you, law of our fathers. I will not forswear you, holy institutions of our ancestors. I will not tarnish you, priestly headbands. I will not openly defile you, my grey hair, with the dust of faithlessness." Why say more? By dying under torture he became a lesson in perseverance for the others, though he had been picked out to be an example of weakness. Blessed, then, is the man in whom torments could not conquer reason. Is he not blessed who, by the strength of his spirit, could triumph over punishment, and with piety as his oar keep his suffering whole amid such waves?

After him seven boys were brought forward with their mother. We may well mock the tyrant. He cunningly thought he should begin with the old man, but he had picked a teacher who would make his pupils braver. Because they were young, as he supposed, he tried to lure them into sin with rewards and to frighten them with threats. But they proved worthy of so great a leader, and answered: "Why do you despise us, or try to trick us as if we were boys? Our faith is grey-haired; our training is strong. Go on, put it to the test. Subject our boyish bodies to whatever punishments you like. You will not find boyish hearts, and your engines of torture will not be stronger than our vigilance in keeping the law. Youth that rivals old age will defeat the man whom old age defeated. As sons we follow our father, as pupils our teacher. Gather up the instruments of torture you have laid out. As we look at them, they give us something to reflect on for endurance, not the terror of the ignorant."

He ordered the eldest to be picked out. But the boy laughed and said: "You rightly keep the order of nature. But why do you think God's law should be violated? When it comes to piety we are all the eldest. Still, I am glad that it begins with me. What do you want, tyrant? I confess that we serve the most high God. And you are teaching us what we ought to do: if you are so determined to wrench the truth from us, why should we not think we must hold on to it with all our strength?" Why say more? Every kind of punishment was applied. But piety conquered the fury of savagery: his soul was driven out, but not his religion.

The second came forward and, worthy of his brother, fulfilled the duty of a holy confession. When the skin was being torn from his head, he answered: "You are taking away the skin, but I have a spiritual helmet that you cannot take away." And truly no one can take away that helmet, as the apostle later taught in the Church of the Lord: the head of man is Christ, and we are his members. The boy rightly foresaw this apostolic teaching by the divine Spirit. Those savage beasts stripped off the crown of his head and raged with the ferocity of leopards. But as he was failing he said: "How sweet it is to die for religion! How pleasant is every bitterness of death for the sake of piety, since a reward for these labours awaits us! Yours are the heavier torments, O king. You are racked more violently by silent tortures, because you see yourself defeated in your very power."

When he was dead, the king ordered the third to be brought before him. He tried him partly with traps and partly hoped to strike him with terror. The boy answered: "I will not do your will or give in to your command. By that blessed suffering and nobility of my brothers, I will not deny the holy bond between us. Apply any tortures you like. The harder you press with cruel punishments, the more you will achieve only this: you will receive greater proofs of our brotherhood." So he ordered his tongue to be cut out. But the boy cried out: "You are beaten, Antiochus, since you order the organ of speech to be cut off. You have admitted that you cannot answer reason, and you show that the lashes of our tongue are heavier than your blows. We do not fear your blows, but you cannot bear the lashes of our voice. Ours are the lashes of piety, yours the lashes of faithlessness. Even when my tongue is taken away, it will lash you more heavily with its murmur as it falls. Do you think you will escape, Antiochus, if you snatch away my voice? God hears even the silent, and hears them all the more. Look, I have opened my mouth and stretched out my tongue. Cut off the tongue, but you will not cut off my constancy. You will not take away my courage, you will not blot out my reason, you will not snatch away the testimony of truth or the cry of the heart. If the tongue is cut off, the blood will cry out, and it will be said to you: 'The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me.' For the one who hears our inward thoughts hears the voice of blood. The wicked man may say, 'Though darkness covers me and walls enclose me,' because no witness stands beside him. But God searches out everything and sees everything, and there is no crime that can be hidden from the Judge of all, who knows all things before they happen. Why spend words? Wounds are more eloquent. Even if the wounds are covered and the scar is hidden, faith is not hidden. Do not congratulate yourself that by taking away the tongue you snatch away our confession of praise. We have praised God enough with words; now let us praise him by suffering."

When he had been killed, the king ordered the fourth to be bound to the wheel, so that its turning would pull all his limbs apart. While he was being savagely tortured, he said: "You are tearing apart the limbs of my body, but you are adding grace to my suffering, and you do not take away the comfort of death." For the voice of thunder is in the wheel, since the heavenly oracle resounds in the good and unhindered course of this life, as it resounded in John and James, the sons of thunder. So I now recognise more clearly what I have read: that the wheel runs within the wheel and is not hindered. A smooth life, without stumbling, keeps turning through any suffering, and within these sufferings too the wheel runs. The law runs within grace, and keeping the law lies within the course of God's mercy; for the more it turns, the more it is proved. "It is better to endure hardship from the wicked here, so that there we may find comfort from the Lord." And he too, finishing his course, broke off his breath and poured out his soul as a victor.

When the fifth was brought forward, the king ordered him first to be beaten, then had fires brought to him and flames lit beneath him. Gore streamed from his wounds, and the blood pouring from his gouged sores put out the very balls of flame. But amid the crackling of the fire he was heard saying: "Thanks be to you, Lord, for granting us to say: 'We have passed through fire.' As your prophet also says elsewhere: 'You have tried us with fire, as silver is tried with fire.' I will stand before you like gold purified by burning, and if there was any guilt, the fire has burned it away." And so he too, transformed from corruption to incorruption, breathed out his life.

Tortures were applied to the sixth as well. But he said: "Do not deceive yourself in vain and credit your own power for being able to do these things to us. This is the price of our sins: we are punished because we have sinned. Thanks be to the Lord that a double penalty for our sins is exacted from us here, so that comfort may be given us there. Thanks to you too, for being so harsh and pitiless, so that through such punishments of ours the Lord, against whom we have sinned, may become gracious to our nation. We ourselves lighten our affliction as we delight in suffering for the faith." And he too, torn apart by harsh and cruel tortures, was laid beside his brothers.

The youngest of the brothers remained. Antiochus was by now ashamed to have been made such a fool of by children so young. So, wanting to trap him with tricks, he promised him honours, riches, his own friendship and a share in his secrets. But the devout mother admonished her son, saying to him what she had said to the others: "I do not know how you came into my womb. It was not I who gave you breath or formed your limbs. These are the gifts of almighty God." Seeing the mother so anxious, Antiochus thought she feared for her son's life, and he too began to urge her to turn her son from his resolve. But she spoke to her son in their ancestral tongue: "You alone are left, my son, the sum of all my prayers. You were the last to close my childbearing; be the last to complete my joys. Have pity on me, who carried you in my womb through so many months. Do not shame my old age in a single moment. Do not tarnish the trophies of all your brothers, do not leave their holy company, do not abandon their fellowship. These triumphs are still waiting for you. Look up to heaven, from which you drew your breath, to the Father of all. Look at the earth, which first gave you nourishment. Look at your brothers, who are looking for their companion. Look at your mother, who gave you milk. Repay what you owe to the blood of your devoted family. Do not be torn away from your brothers or from your mother. The riches Antiochus promises are temporary, and so are his honours; but the crown that almighty God bestows is everlasting. The Lord gave me the light of seven days. I have already brought the sixth day to its close, and all their works are very good. You owe it to me, my son, that what I laboured over in those six, I may rest in you on the seventh, as one now free from the works of this world." At that the young man rushed forward and said: "What are you waiting for?" He cried out at length that he could never be torn from the fellowship of his brothers, whose deaths were far more blessed than a king's commands. As he pressed the king with reproaches, he too was tormented with bitter kinds of torture and completed the task of this life.

Last of all, the mother was brought to her death. Who would deny that she was blessed? It was as if she were fortified by seven walls as she stood among the bodies of her sons, feeling no assault of death. Who, I say, would doubt the blessedness of her who, surrounded by seven towers, raised her head to the seat of paradise? Girded by her seven sons, she brought to the heavenly altars a choir most holy to God, tuneful not only with voices but also with sufferings, to sing the praises of the Lord together. How good a fruit of faith she bore! How safe a harbour of piety she was! How splendid a lamp of the Church, shining with a sevenfold light and, as the eighth, from her womb supplying oil to all the lights! Of them it is beautifully said: "Give a portion to those seven, and also to those eight." For in both numbers they gain a share in grace: nourished in the law, crowned through grace, seven as in the sabbath, eight as in the gospel. Their devoted mother was joined to them to complete their suffering. In such sons she both conceived and brought forth the perfect pattern of piety.

The words of that holy woman come back to mind, when she said to her sons: "I bore you, I poured the milk into you: do not lose your nobility." Other mothers say such things to call their sons back from martyrdom, not to call them to it. But she showed a mother's love in this: in urging on her sons a life that is everlasting rather than one that is temporary. So the devoted mother watched her sons' contests. Although she was shaken to the depths of her mother's heart, she suppressed her grief out of zeal for piety. When Antiochus made his offer, she could have chosen her sons' safety, but she preferred their danger. Stifling the groans of nature, she wished their punishment increased so that death might come sooner. We see a mother's wishes [?] for her sons turned upside down: she wanted to leave none of them alive, but to win them all as fellow heirs of a holy death.

Nor were the sons any less than such a mother. They encouraged one another, saying with a single zeal and like a battle line of spirits: "Let us crush the onslaught of hostile death. For then we shall live, when we have died. Let no one desert the ranks of piety; let no one withdraw from the battle of triumph. We have devoted our souls not to a man but to almighty God. We are soldiers not for a man but for the Author of all things. This battle is such that whoever is killed more cruelly wins more gloriously." So no one feared, no one trembled. Not one of all those brothers was slow to face death; all ran to death through bitter tortures as if on the road to immortality. And the mother, seeing the ranks of her sons in harmony, offered in her sons the members of her own body, like a devoted soul, and seemed to herself to be undergoing through her own limbs the torments she had willingly offered.

Her sons were falling, their bodies torn open by torture. The dead were rolled upon the dead, bodies tumbled upon bodies, heads were cut off one upon another, and the place was filled with the corpses of her sons. The mother did not weep. She did not lament. She did not close anyone's eyes or the mouth of any who were dying. She did not wash their wounds, knowing that they were more glorious if they were seen torn open and caked with dust and blood, as victors usually return from war, as those who carry home trophies taken from the enemy. She did not think they should be covered with shrouds or given funeral rites, except with her own death to accompany them. What lyre could have produced sweeter songs than those her sons uttered as they exhorted one another [?] amid such heavy tortures? For the groan of nature burst out even from the unwilling. You could see the corpses of the slain laid out in order like the strings of a lyre; you could hear a seven-stringed psaltery resounding with triumphant groans. Not even the alluring songs of the Sirens, as they call them, would draw a listener like this; for they drew men to shipwreck, but these drew them to the victory of sacrifice. Nor would swan songs so charm the ears and the mind; for swans die by the lot of nature, but these died for love of piety. The hoarse murmurs of doves in a secluded grove do not resound so sweetly as the last words of the dying resounded. Nor does the moon shine among the stars as the mother shone among her sons, both when she led them to martyrdom to make them radiant, and when she lay in their midst, embracing the victors.

O mother, truly stronger than adamant, sweeter than honey, more fragrant than a flower! O unbreakable bond of piety! O love, truly as strong as death! O zeal of devotion and faith, as hard as the grave! No floods of such terrible sufferings could shut out your love, no rivers of such bitterness could overflow it. As the ark in that flood of the world was carried unharmed across the expanse of the whole earth, so you too stood firm against the flood of such grievous sufferings, kept steady by piety. You could have chosen your sons' safety, but you would not. With what love shall I honour you, holy children of a holy mother? With what brush of speech shall I portray the likeness of your bodies and your souls? You stood amid the royal armies that had subdued the whole world, armies that even India avoided by fleeing into the hidden reaches of the farthest sea. You alone, without any battle, won victory over the proud king. In you the arms of piety alone were victorious. The tyrant paid the penalty, both because he could not conquer you and because he perished by a dreadful death.
